entities.summary:
The Second Boer War (1899-1902) was a pivotal conflict between the two Boer republics, the South African Republic and the Orange Free State, and the United Kingdom. This war was sparked by the desire of the Boers to maintain their independence and self-governance in the face of British expansionism in South Africa. The war saw the deployment of over 450,000 British troops and the use of concentration camps, which would later become infamous for their inhumane conditions.

The war began on October 23, 1899, with the Battle of Talana Hill, and it would go on to last for three years, resulting in the deaths of over 22,000 Boer soldiers and 22,000 black South African soldiers. The conflict ended on May 31, 1902, with the signing of the Treaty of Vereeniging, which led to the establishment of a British-dominated government in South Africa.

The Second Boer War had significant consequences for the people of South Africa, leading to the loss of their land and culture. It also marked the beginning of a period of British dominance in South Africa, which would last for over 40 years.

The Second Boer War will be remembered as a turning point in the history of South Africa, marking the end of the Boer's struggle for independence and the beginning of a new era under British rule.
